title: De Spielhansl
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 1, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 82. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original). 1857 spelling preserved exactly. This tale is in South German (Bavarian-Austrian) dialect; the glossary gives the High German equivalent for each dialect form. The glosses in round brackets inside the text — wal (weil), Hietzt (jetzt) — are the Grimms’ own and belong to the 1857 text.
about: KHM 82, told from beginning to end in a South German (Bavarian-Austrian) dialect — not the Low German of the fisherman’s tale and the juniper tree but the speech of the far south, so that nearly every word looks a little foreign beside the High German of the rest of the collection. A man who has gambled away his house lodges our Lord God and Saint Peter, and when he is offered three wishes he asks not for heaven but for cards and dice that always win and a tree nobody can climb down from. He strands Death up in it for seven years, so that no one on earth can die; and when he is throttled at last, heaven, purgatory and hell turn him away in turn. Grimm glosses the hardest dialect words in parentheses inside the 1857 text itself — wal (weil), Hietzt (jetzt) — and those parentheses are his, not ours.

sentences.t: Is is emohl e Mon gewön, der hot ninx us (als) g’spielt, und do hobend’n d’ Leut nur in Spielhansl g’hoaßen,
sentences.l: There has once been a man, he has done nothing but (als) gamble, and so the people called him nothing but the Spielhansl,
sentences.i: There was once a man who did nothing but gamble, and so people called him nothing but Spielhansl, Gambling Hansl,
sentences.n: This tale is printed in the Bavarian-Austrian dialect of the south, and the Grimms gloss the hardest words themselves inside the text: the round brackets and the High German words standing in them — us (als) here, then wal (weil), Hietzt (jetzt), iahm (ihm) — are the Grimms’ own, part of the 1857 text, and they are kept in the English too. Is is = es ist, emohl = einmal, e = ein, Mon = Mann, gewön = gewesen, hot = hat, ninx = nichts, hobend’n = haben ihn, d’ Leut = die Leute, in = den, g’hoaßen = geheißen. The whole tale is told in the perfect — “ist gewesen,” “hat gespielt” — as southern speech does where the north would use the simple past. spielen throughout means to gamble.

sentences.t: und wal (weil) e gor nit afg’hört zen spieln, se hot e san (sein) Haus und ullss (alles) vespielt.
sentences.l: and because (weil) he did not leave off gambling at all, so he gambled away his (sein) house and everything (alles).
sentences.i: and because he would not leave off gambling at all, he gambled away his house and all he had.
sentences.n: gor nit = gar nicht, not at all; afg’hört = aufgehört. zen spieln = zu spielen — zen does duty for zu all through the tale. se = so, the resuming “then” after a because-clause. verspielen is to lose at play, to gamble away.

sentences.t: Hietzt (jetzt), nette (eben) in lötzten Tog, eh’s iahm (ihm) d’ Schuldne schon s’ Haus hobend wögnehme willn, is unse Herrgout un de halli Pedrus kemme und hobend g’sogt er sull’s übe d’ Nacht g’holte (bei sich behalten).
sentences.l: Now (jetzt), just (eben) on the last day, before the creditors were going to take the house from him (ihm), our Lord God and Saint Peter came and said he should keep them over the night (bei sich behalten).
sentences.i: Now, on the very last day, before his creditors could take the house away from him, our Lord God and Saint Peter came and said he should keep them over the night.
sentences.n: d’ Schuldne are the men he owes — his creditors. eh’s = ehe es; “hobend wögnehme willn” is the southern perfect with a double infinitive, haben wegnehmen wollen. de halli Pedrus = der heilige Petrus, Saint Peter, who walks the earth with the Lord in many of these tales. lötzten = letzten, Tog = Tag.

sentences.t: Oft (da) hot de Spielhansl g’sogt „wögn meine kints do bleibn döi Nocht; ober i kong eng koan Bött und ninx z’össn (zu essen) gebn.“
sentences.l: Then (da) the Spielhansl said “for all I care you can stay the night here; but I can give you no bed and nothing to eat (zu essen).”
sentences.i: Then Spielhansl said: “For my part you may stay the night; but I can give you no bed and nothing to eat.”
sentences.n: Oft (da) is this tale’s constant “then,” and the Grimms gloss it the first time. “wögn meine” = wegen meiner, for all I care, as far as I am concerned. kints = könnt’s, that is könnt ihr — the pronoun swallowed into the verb, which will keep happening. eng = euch, koan = kein, Bött = Bett, Nocht = Nacht.

sentences.t: Oft hot unse Herrgout g’sogt er sulls ne (nur) g’holten, und söi willetn ian (ihnen) selbe wos z’össn kaffen;
sentences.l: Then our Lord God said he should just (nur) keep them, and they would buy themselves (ihnen) something to eat;
sentences.i: Then our Lord God said he need only take them in, and they would buy themselves something to eat;
sentences.n: sulls = soll sie; ne (nur) = just, only. willetn is the subjunctive of reported speech, southern for wollten — they would buy; kaffen = kaufen. The Grimms gloss ian with (ihnen), the dative.

sentences.t: dos is in Spielhansl recht g’wön.
sentences.l: that was right to the Spielhansl.
sentences.i: that suited Spielhansl well enough.
sentences.n: “jemandem recht sein” = to be all right by someone; in Spielhansl is dative, with the southern article in for dem. dos = das, g’wön = gewesen.

sentences.t: Oft hot iahm de halli Pedrus drei Grouschn gebn, und er sull zen Böcke (Becker) gehn und e Brod huhln.
sentences.l: Then Saint Peter gave him three Groschen, and he should go to the baker (Becker) and fetch a loaf.
sentences.i: Then Saint Peter gave him three groschen, and he was to go to the baker and fetch a loaf.
sentences.n: A Groschen was a small coin worth a few pennies — enough for bread and no more. “er sull … gehn” is reported speech with no verb of saying in front of it: he was to go. huhln = holen, Brod = Brot. Böcke is the southern Beck, baker, which the Grimms gloss with Becker.

sentences.t: Hietzt is hullt (halt) de Spielhansl gonge, wie er aber ze den Haus kemme is, wou die onnen Spiellumpn drin g’wön sand, döi iahm ullss ogwunge hobnd,
sentences.l: Now the Spielhansl went then (halt); but when he came to the house where the other gambling-rascals were inside, who had won everything off him,
sentences.i: So off Spielhansl went; but when he came to the house where the other gambling rogues were sitting, the ones who had won everything off him,
sentences.n: hullt (here glossed halt) is the southern particle of resignation — just, simply; it has no English word, and is carried through this tale by a light “then.” Spiellumpn are Lumpen, ragamuffins, who gamble. “ogwunge” = abgewonnen, and abgewinnen takes the dative of the loser: to win a thing off someone. sand = sind, döi = die.

sentences.t: do hob’ns n g’ruefft und hobend g’schrien „Hansl, geh ahne (herein).“
sentences.l: there they called him and cried “Hansl, come in (herein).”
sentences.i: they called out to him and shouted: “Hansl, come inside!”
sentences.n: hob’ns = haben sie, the same swallowed pronoun as in kints; n = ihn. g’ruefft = gerufen, g’schrien = geschrien. ahne = herein, one of the little direction-words — ahne, anhi, ausse, affi, ohi — that carry much of this dialect’s motion, and which the Grimms gloss as they come.

sentences.t: „Jo,“ hot e g’sogt, „willt’s me die drei Grouschn a non ogwinge.“
sentences.l: “Yes,” he said, “you want to win the three Groschen off me as well.”
sentences.i: “Oh yes,” he said, “you want to win my three groschen off me too.”
sentences.n: willt’s = wollt ihr, again with the pronoun taken into the verb. me = mir, a = auch, non = noch. There is no question mark: it is half question, half resignation, and he goes in.

sentences.t: Döi hobnd’n obe (aber) nit ausg’lossn.
sentences.l: But (aber) they did not let him out.
sentences.i: But they would not let him go.
sentences.n: auslassen here is to let someone out, let him off — they will not. hobnd’n = haben ihn; obe is glossed with (aber) at its first appearance and then left to stand.

sentences.t: Hietzt is e hullt anhi (hinein) und oft hot e die drei Grouschn a non vespielt.
sentences.l: Now he was in (hinein) then, and then he gambled the three Groschen away as well.
sentences.i: So in he went, and then he gambled the three groschen away as well.
sentences.n: The verb of motion is left out altogether — “is e hullt anhi,” he simply is “in” — which southern speech does freely with these direction-words. anhi = hinein.

sentences.t: De halli Pedrus und unse Herrgout hobnd ollewall (immer) g’wort’t, und wie er ian z’long nit kemme is, sand’s iahm intgögn gonge.
sentences.l: Saint Peter and our Lord God had waited all the while (immer), and when he did not come for too long for them, they went to meet him.
sentences.i: Saint Peter and our Lord God waited and waited; and when he was too long in coming for them, they went out to meet him.
sentences.n: ollewall (immer) = all the time, all the while. “ian z’long” = ihnen zu lang, too long for them, with the dative of the people kept waiting. g’wort’t = gewartet; “intgögn gonge” = entgegengegangen; sand’s = sind sie.

sentences.t: De Spielhansl obe, wie e kemme is, hot thon us wenn iahm’s Geld in ne Locken (Lacken) g’folln war, und hot ollewall drin herumkrobbelt:
sentences.l: But the Spielhansl, when he came, did as if the money had fallen into a puddle (Lacken) for him, and kept scrabbling about in it:
sentences.i: But Spielhansl, when he came up, made out that the money had fallen into a puddle, and kept groping about in it;
sentences.n: “hot thon us wenn” = hat getan als wenn, made as though; iahm’s = ihm das, with the dative of the man it befell. Lacken is the Austrian word for a puddle or pool, which the Grimms set in brackets to explain Locken. herumkrobbelt = herumgekrabbelt, scrabbled about. He is miming a search for coins he has in fact gambled away.

sentences.t: obe unse Herrgout hots schon g’wißt, daß e’s vespielt hot.
sentences.l: but our Lord God had known all along that he had gambled it away.
sentences.i: but our Lord God knew well enough that he had gambled it away.
sentences.n: hots = hat es, e’s = er es. schon here is “well enough, all along,” not “already.” g’wißt = gewußt.

sentences.t: Oft hot iahm de halli Pedrus non mohl drei Grouschn gebn.
sentences.l: Then Saint Peter gave him three Groschen once more.
sentences.i: Then Saint Peter gave him another three groschen.
sentences.n: “non mohl” = noch mal, once again. That the saint pays twice is part of the joke — the gambler is trusted a second time.

sentences.t: Hietzt hot e sie obe nimme veführn losse und hot ian s’ Brod brocht.
sentences.l: Now he did not let himself be led astray any more and brought them the bread.
sentences.i: This time he did not let himself be led astray, and brought them the bread.
sentences.n: nimme = nimmer, never again, no more. sie here is the reflexive sich in southern form, and “veführn losse” = verführen lassen, to let oneself be led astray. ian = ihnen, s’ = das.

sentences.t: Oft hot’n unse Herrgout g’frogt wou e koan’n Wein nit hot, do hot e g’sogt „u, Herr, d’ Fasse sand alli laar.“
sentences.l: Then our Lord God asked him why he had no wine, and he said “oh, Lord, the casks are all empty.”
sentences.i: Then our Lord God asked him how it was he had no wine, and he said: “Oh, Lord, the casks are all empty.”
sentences.n: wou here is not “where” but warum, why — the dialect uses the one word for both. “koan’n Wein nit” piles two negatives to make one, which is ordinary southern speech and no mistake. Fasse = Fässer, laar = leer, alli = alle, u = the exclamation oh.

sentences.t: Oft hot unse Herrgout g’sogt er sull ner in Költe (Keller) ohi (hinab) gehn, „is is non de böst Wein int.“
sentences.l: Then our Lord God said he should just go down (hinab) into the cellar (Keller), “there is still the best wine in it.”
sentences.i: Then our Lord God told him just to go down into the cellar: “the best wine is still down there.”
sentences.n: ner = nur, just. int = drinnen, in there; “is is” = es ist. The sentence begins as reported speech and slips into direct speech in mid-course, as a spoken telling does. The Grimms gloss both Költe (Keller) and ohi (hinab).

sentences.t: Er hots long nit glaubn willn, obe af d’löst hot e g’sogt „i will ohi gehn, ober i woaß’s daß koane int is.“
sentences.l: He would not believe it for a long time, but at the last he said “I will go down, but I know it that there is none in there.”
sentences.i: For a long time he would not believe it, but at last he said: “I will go down, but I know there is none there.”
sentences.n: “af d’löst” = auf die Letzt, at last, in the end. “hots … glaubn willn” is again the southern perfect with the double infinitive, hat es glauben wollen. woaß’s = weiß es, koane = keiner, not a drop.

sentences.t: Wie er obe’s Fassl onzapft hot, se is de böst Wein ausse g’runne.
sentences.l: But when he tapped the little cask, then the best wine ran out.
sentences.i: But when he broached the little cask, out ran the best wine.
sentences.n: Fassl is the diminutive of Faß, a little cask. anzapfen = to tap, to broach a barrel. “ausse g’runne” = herausgeronnen, ran out; se = so, the resuming “then.”

sentences.t: Hietzt hot er ian in Wein brocht, und döi zwoa sand übe d’ Nocht do blieb’n.
sentences.l: Now he brought them the wine, and those two stayed there over the night.
sentences.i: So he brought them the wine, and the two of them stayed the night there.
sentences.n: in Wein is accusative, with the southern in for den. zwoa = zwei, blieb’n = geblieben, übe = über.

sentences.t: In onnen Tog, in de Früe, hot unse Herrgout zen Spielhansl g’sogt, er sull sie (sich) drei Gnodn ausbittn.
sentences.l: The next day, in the early morning, our Lord God said to the Spielhansl he should ask for himself (sich) three graces.
sentences.i: Next day, early in the morning, our Lord God told Spielhansl to ask three favours for himself.
sentences.n: “in onnen Tog” = am andern Tag, on the next day; “in de Früe” = in der Frühe, early in the morning. Gnaden are graces, favours granted from above; “sich ausbitten” is to ask a favour for oneself, separable aus-. The Grimms gloss sie with (sich) because in this dialect sie also serves as the reflexive.

sentences.t: Er hot g’moant, er wird sie ’n Himmel ausbittn, obe de Spielhansl hot bettn um e Korntn, mit der er ullss g’wingt;
sentences.l: He thought he would ask heaven for himself, but the Spielhansl asked for a pack of cards with which he wins everything;
sentences.i: He supposed the man would ask for heaven; but Spielhansl asked for a pack of cards that would win him everything,
sentences.n: meinen here is to suppose, to expect. bettn = gebeten, and “bitten um” = to ask for. Korntn is the dialect Karten, playing cards. The wish is exactly what a gambler would ask and nothing more — the tale lets Saint Peter’s expectation stand next to it without comment.

sentences.t: um Würfl, mit den er a ullss g’wingt, und um en Bam (Baum), wou ullss Oubst draf wochst,
sentences.l: for dice with which he also wins everything, and for a tree (Baum) on which all fruit grows,
sentences.i: for dice that would win him everything too, and for a tree with every kind of fruit growing on it,
sentences.n: Würfl = Würfel, dice. “wou … draf” = wo … darauf, on which — wou again serves as a general relative particle. Oubst = Obst, wochst = wächst, en Bam = einen Baum.

sentences.t: und wonn oane (einer) affi steigt, daß e nimme ohe kon (herab kann), bis er iahm’s schofft (befiehlt).
sentences.l: and that when someone (einer) climbs up, he can no longer get down (herab kann) until he orders it of him (befiehlt).
sentences.i: and that whoever climbed up should not be able to get down again until he gave him leave.
sentences.n: Three of the Grimms’ own glosses stand together here: oane (einer), kon (herab kann), schofft (befiehlt). schaffen in the south means to order, to command, not to work or to make. affi = hinauf, ohe = herab, nimme = nimmer. The wish sounds idle and is the one that will catch Death.

sentences.t: Hietzt hot iahm unse Herrgout ullss gebn, wos e velangt hot un is mit’n hallin Pedrus wiede fuert (fort).
sentences.l: Now our Lord God gave him everything that he demanded, and went away again (fort) with Saint Peter.
sentences.i: So our Lord God gave him everything he asked for, and went off again with Saint Peter.
sentences.n: wos = was, the relative “what, that which.” “is … wiede fuert” once more leaves out the verb of motion: is away again. “mit’n hallin Pedrus” = mit dem heiligen Petrus, dative; un = und.

sentences.t: Hietzt hot hult de Spielhansl erst recht zen spieln ongfongt, und hätt bold d’ halbeti Welt zomg’wunge.
sentences.l: Now the Spielhansl began to gamble in good earnest, and had soon won half the world together.
sentences.i: Now Spielhansl set about his gambling in good earnest, and had soon raked in half the world.
sentences.n: “erst recht” = all the more, now more than ever. ongfongt = angefangen, halbeti = halbe, zomg’wunge = zusammengewonnen — won together, raked in. hätt is the southern perfect auxiliary where we should say hatte.

sentences.t: Oft hot de halli Pedrus ze’n unse Herrgoutn g’sogt „Herr, dos Ding thuet koan guet, er g’winget af d’löst non (noch) d’ganzi Welt;
sentences.l: Then Saint Peter said to our Lord God “Lord, this thing does no good, in the end he still (noch) wins the whole world;
sentences.i: Then Saint Peter said to our Lord God: “Lord, this will come to no good — in the end he will win the whole world;
sentences.n: “dos Ding thuet koan guet” = das Ding tut kein gut, this business will turn out badly — Saint Peter’s refrain, and he will say it twice more. thuet = tut, g’winget = gewinnt, ganzi = ganze. “af d’löst” = at the last, as before.

sentences.t: me müssn iahm in (den) Toid schickn.“
sentences.l: we must send Death (den) to him.”
sentences.n: me = wir; müssn = müssen. Toid = Tod, Death, who comes as a person in these tales and can be sent on an errand. The Grimms gloss in with (den), the accusative article.

sentences.t: Hietzt habend’s iahm in Toid g’schickt.
sentences.l: Now they sent Death to him.
sentences.n: habend’s = haben sie, with the pronoun swallowed into the verb once more; g’schickt = geschickt.

sentences.t: Wie de Toid kemme is, is de Spielhansl nette be’n Spieltisch g’sössn;
sentences.l: When Death came, the Spielhansl was just sitting at the gaming-table;
sentences.i: When Death came, Spielhansl was sitting at the gaming table;
sentences.n: nette = eben, just, precisely — glossed by the Grimms at its first appearance early in the tale. g’sössn = gesessen.

sentences.t: oft hot de Toid g’sogt „Hansl, kimm e Bissl ausse.“
sentences.l: then Death said “Hansl, come out a little.”
sentences.i: then Death said: “Hansl, step outside a moment.”
sentences.n: kimm = komm, the imperative. “e Bissl” = ein bißchen, a little; ausse = heraus. Death is politeness itself, and asks him to step out — which is all the opening the gambler needs.

sentences.t: De Spielhansl obe hot g’sogt „wort nur e Bissl, bis dos G’spiel aus is,
sentences.l: But the Spielhansl said “only wait a little, until the game is over,
sentences.i: But Spielhansl said: “Only wait a bit, till the game is over,
sentences.n: “bis dos G’spiel aus is” = bis das Spiel aus ist, until the game is finished — G’spiel is the southern Spiel with its g- prefix. wort = warte, the imperative.

sentences.t: und steig dewall e weng af’n Bam do affi und brouck uns e wengerl wos o, daß me afn Wög wos z’noschn hobn.“
sentences.l: and climb meanwhile a bit up the tree there and break us off a little something, so that we have something to nibble on the way.”
sentences.i: and climb up that tree there meanwhile and pick us off a little something, so that we have a bite to eat on the way.”
sentences.n: dewall = derweil, meanwhile. “e weng” and “e wengerl” = ein wenig and its diminutive, a little and a little bit. brouck = brock ab, pick, break off; “wos o” = etwas ab, with the separable prefix at the end. “z’noschn” = zu naschen, to nibble at sweet things. This is the tree of the third wish, and Death climbs it without a thought.

sentences.t: Hietzt is hullt de Toid affi g’stiegn, und wie e wiede hot ohi wille, hot e nit kinne,
sentences.l: Now Death climbed up then, and when he wanted to come down again, he could not,
sentences.i: So up Death climbed; and when he wanted to come down again, he could not,
sentences.n: “hot ohi wille” = hat hinab wollen, wanted to go down, with the verb of motion again left out; “hot e nit kinne” = hat er nicht können, he has not been able — the southern perfect of the modal standing alone.

sentences.t: und de Spielhansl hot’n sieben Johr droubn lossn, und dewall is koan Mensch nit g’storbn.
sentences.l: and the Spielhansl left him up there seven years, and meanwhile not a single person died.
sentences.i: and Spielhansl left him up there seven years, and in all that while not one person died.
sentences.n: droubn = droben, up there; “koan Mensch nit g’storbn” doubles the negative again for emphasis: no one at all died. Seven years is the tale’s round number for a long time.

sentences.t: Oft hot de halli Pedrus zen unsen Herrgoutn g’sagt „Herr, dos Ding thuet koan guet, is sterbet jo koan Mensch mehr;
sentences.l: Then Saint Peter said to our Lord God “Lord, this thing does no good, why, not a soul dies any more;
sentences.i: Then Saint Peter said to our Lord God: “Lord, this will come to no good — not a soul dies any more;
sentences.n: Saint Peter’s refrain comes round for the second time, word for word. “is sterbet jo koan Mensch mehr” = es stirbt ja kein Mensch mehr, with jo (ja) the little word of appeal — why, as you see. g’sagt here, g’sogt elsewhere: the printing keeps both spellings.

sentences.t: mir müessn schon selbe kemme.“
sentences.l: we must come ourselves now.”
sentences.i: we shall have to go ourselves.”
sentences.n: müessn = müssen; selbe = selber, ourselves. schon here urges rather than dates anything — we really must.

sentences.t: Hietzt sand’s hullt selbe kemme, und do hot iahm unse Herrgout g’schofft daß er in Toid ohe lossn sull.
sentences.l: Now they came themselves then, and there our Lord God ordered him that he should let Death down.
sentences.i: So they came themselves, and there our Lord God ordered him to let Death down.
sentences.n: g’schofft is schaffen in its southern sense of commanding — the same verb the third wish used (schofft, glossed befiehlt). “in Toid ohe lossn” = den Tod herab lassen, to let Death down out of the tree; ohe = herab.

sentences.t: Oft is er obe glei gonge und hot zen Toid g’sogt „geh ohe,“ und der hot’n glei g’numme und hot’n okragelt (erwürgt).
sentences.l: But then he went at once and said to Death “go down,” and he took him at once and throttled him (erwürgt).
sentences.i: Then he went at once and said to Death, “Come down,” and Death took him at once and throttled him.
sentences.n: okragelt is the dialect verb the Grimms gloss with erwürgt, to strangle — abkrageln, from Kragen, the neck. der at the head of the second half is a demonstrative, “that one,” and it is Death: released, he kills the gambler on the spot. glei = gleich, at once; g’numme = genommen.

sentences.t: Oft sands mit enonne fuert und sand in d’ onneri Welt kemme,
sentences.l: Then they went off with one another and came into the other world,
sentences.i: Then off they went together and came into the other world,
sentences.n: enonne = einander; “sands … fuert” leaves out the verb of motion again — they are away. “d’ onneri Welt” = die andere Welt, the next world.

sentences.t: do is hullt man (mein) Spielhansl zen Himmelthoir gonge und hot onkloupft.
sentences.l: there my (mein) Spielhansl went to the heaven-door then and knocked.
sentences.i: and there my Spielhansl went up to the door of heaven and knocked.
sentences.n: “man (mein) Spielhansl” — the teller calls him my Spielhansl, the affectionate possessive a story-teller uses of a rogue he is fond of, and the Grimms gloss man with mein. Himmelthoir = Himmelstor, the gate of heaven; onkloupft = angeklopft.

sentences.t: „Wer is draußt?“ „De Spielhansl.“
sentences.l: “Who is outside?” “The Spielhansl.”
sentences.i: “Who is out there?” “Spielhansl.”
sentences.n: draußt = draußen. The three gates — heaven, purgatory, hell — are knocked at in the same words each time, and the answer is always the bare name; the tale is built on the repetition.

sentences.t: „Ach, den brauche me nit, geh ne wiede fuert.“
sentences.l: “Ah, him we do not need, just go away again.”
sentences.i: “Ah, we have no use for him — off with you again.”
sentences.n: den is the accusative demonstrative, “that one, him,” standing first for emphasis. me = wir; ne = nur, just; “geh ne wiede fuert” = geh nur wieder fort.

sentences.t: Oft is e zen Fegfuirthoir gonge und hot wiede kloupft.
sentences.l: Then he went to the purgatory-door and knocked again.
sentences.i: Then he went to the door of purgatory and knocked again.
sentences.n: Fegfuirthoir = Fegfeuertor, the gate of purgatory — the middle place of Catholic teaching, between heaven and hell, which is why the tale has three doors and not two.

sentences.t: „Wer is draußt?“ „De Spielhansl.“
sentences.l: “Who is outside?” “The Spielhansl.”
sentences.i: “Who is out there?” “Spielhansl.”
sentences.n: The same exchange, word for word — the second of three.

sentences.t: „Ach, is is e so (ohne das) Jomme und Noith g’nue be’n uns, mir willn nit spieln; geh ne wiede fuert.“
sentences.l: “Ah, there is misery and want enough with us as it is (ohne das), we do not want to gamble; just go away again.”
sentences.i: “Ah, there is grief and misery enough here without that; we have no wish to gamble. Off with you again.”
sentences.n: “e so” = eh so, anyway, in any case, and the Grimms gloss it with ohne das, without that. Jomme = Jammer, Noith = Not (the 1857 spelling keeps th), g’nue = genug, “be’n uns” = bei uns.

sentences.t: Of is e zen Hüllnthoir gonge, und do hobn’s n anhi lossn,
sentences.l: Then he went to the hell-door, and there they let him in,
sentences.i: Then he went to the door of hell, and there they let him in,
sentences.n: Hüllnthoir = Höllentor. Of at the head of the sentence is the same Oft (da) as everywhere else, with the t dropped in the printing. anhi = hinein, as at the gambling house.

sentences.t: is is obe niamd dehoambt g’wön, us de olti Luzifar und krumpn Tuifln (die g’rodn hobn af de Welt z’ thoan g’hot),
sentences.l: but nobody was at home, except old Lucifer and crooked devils (the straight ones had business out in the world),
sentences.i: but there was nobody at home except old Lucifer and some crooked devils — the straight ones had business out in the world —
sentences.n: niamd = niemand, dehoambt = daheim, us = als in the sense of except. This parenthesis is not a High German gloss like the others but an aside of the tale’s own. I read “die g’rodn” as die geraden, the straight or sound devils, who are out on the world’s business, leaving only the crooked ones at home. Two things point that way: hobn stands second, so “die g’rodn” is the subject of a main clause and not a relative “die … gerade,” which would push the verb to the end; and the whole joke of what Lucifer has left to stake depends on straight devils being away and crooked ones at home. The other reading, gerade as “just then,” would have to say that the devils who were at home were the ones with business elsewhere, which is why I have not taken it — but the word is dialect and I record the doubt.

sentences.t: und oft hot e si glei ine (nieder) g’sötzt und hot wiede zen spieln ong’fongt.
sentences.l: and then he sat himself down (nieder) at once and began to gamble again.
sentences.i: and he sat himself down at once and began to gamble again.
sentences.n: si = sich, g’sötzt = gesetzt; ine is glossed by the Grimms with nieder, down. He is in hell and the first thing he does is deal.

sentences.t: Hietzt hot obe de Luzifar ninx g’hot, us sani krumpn Tuifln:
sentences.l: But now Lucifer had nothing but his crooked devils:
sentences.i: Now Lucifer had nothing to stake but his crooked devils;
sentences.n: us again = als, nothing but. sani = seine. What a man has is what he can stake — and Lucifer’s whole property, at this hour, is the lame devils left at home.

sentences.t: döi hot iahm de Spielhansl ogwunge, wall e mit sann Kortn ulls hot g’winge müeßn.
sentences.l: those the Spielhansl won off him, because with his cards he had to win everything.
sentences.i: and those Spielhansl won off him, because with his cards he could not help winning everything.
sentences.n: wall = weil, sann = seinen, Kortn = Karten. “hot g’winge müeßn” = hat gewinnen müssen, the southern perfect with the double infinitive: he was bound to win — the first wish working on its own, whether he will or no.

sentences.t: Hietzt is e mit sann krumpn Tuifln fuert, und oft sand’s af Hoihefuert (nach Hohenfurt),
sentences.l: Now he went off with his crooked devils, and then they were away to Hohenfurt (nach Hohenfurt),
sentences.i: So off he went with his crooked devils, and then they made for Hohenfurt,
sentences.n: Hoihefuert is the dialect name the Grimms gloss as Hohenfurt — the market town in southern Bohemia, in the country where this tale was told; naming a real place is part of the fun. The verb of motion is left out once more: sand’s af = they are off to.

sentences.t: und hobnd d’ Houpfnstange ausg’rissn und san demit zen Himml affi und hobnd zen wägn ong’fongt;
sentences.l: and tore out the hop-poles and were up to heaven with them and began to lever;
sentences.i: and they tore up the hop-poles and were off up to heaven with them and set about prising it open;
sentences.n: Houpfnstange = Hopfenstangen, the long poles a hop-garden is grown on — the tallest things at hand. “zen wägn” I take as zu wegen, to lever, to prise with a bar, which is what poles are for and what makes heaven crack in the next breath. The spelling supports it: this text writes a as o throughout (Tog, Nocht, hobn, gonge), so wagen would appear as wogn, and the ä of wägn must stand for a front vowel, that is wegen. The verb is dialect and I record the doubt, but the reading is not an even guess. ausg’rissn = ausgerissen, demit = damit, affi = hinauf.

sentences.t: und hietzt hot de Himml schon krocht (gekracht).
sentences.l: and now heaven was already cracking (gekracht).
sentences.i: and by now heaven was cracking already.
sentences.n: krocht is glossed by the Grimms with gekracht — the noise of timber giving way. schon = already, at this point.

sentences.t: Oft hot de halli Pedrus wiede g’sogt „Herr, dos Ding thuet koan guet, mir müeßn ne anhe (herein) lossn, sunst werfet er uns in Himmel ohi (hinab).“
sentences.l: Then Saint Peter said again “Lord, this thing does no good, we must just let him in (herein), otherwise he throws us down (hinab) out of heaven.”
sentences.i: Then Saint Peter said again: “Lord, this will come to no good — we must let him in, or he will throw us out of heaven.”
sentences.n: The refrain a third time, and now it argues the other way: heaven must open to him to save itself. ne is the nur the Grimms glossed earlier — we must just let him in — with the object left unspoken, as this dialect does freely. sunst = sonst, werfet = wirft. The Grimms gloss the two direction-words in one sentence, anhe (herein) and ohi (hinab), which between them hold the whole quarrel.

sentences.t: Hietzt hobnd’s ’n hult anhi lossn.
sentences.l: Now they let him in then.
sentences.i: So they let him in.
sentences.n: hobnd’s = haben sie, ’n = ihn. The gambler is in heaven, and by force.

sentences.t: Obe de Spielhansl hot glei wiede zen spieln ong’fongt, und do is glei e Lärm un e Getös won (worden), daß me san oagns Wort nit vestondn hot.
sentences.l: But the Spielhansl began to gamble again at once, and then there arose (worden) such a noise and such an uproar that one could not understand one’s own word.
sentences.i: But Spielhansl set to gambling again at once, and there was such a noise and uproar that no one could hear his own voice.
sentences.n: won is glossed by the Grimms with worden: “is … won” = ist geworden, there arose. “san oagns Wort” = sein eigenes Wort, one’s own word; me = man, one. Getös = Getöse, din.

sentences.t: Oft hat de halli Pedrus wiede g’sogt „Herr, dos Ding thuet koan guet, wir müßn ne ohi werfen, er machet uns sunst in gonzn Himl rewellisch.“
sentences.l: Then Saint Peter said again “Lord, this thing does no good, we must just throw him down, otherwise he makes the whole heaven riotous for us.”
sentences.i: Then Saint Peter said again: “Lord, this will come to no good — we must throw him out, or he will turn the whole of heaven upside down on us.”
sentences.n: The refrain for the fourth and last time. rewellisch is from Rebell, riotous, mutinous — to make a place rewellisch is to turn it upside down. machet = macht, gonzn = ganzen, Himl = Himmel. uns is the dative of the people it is done to, which English can only render as “on us.”

sentences.t: Hietzt sands hullt her und hobnd’n ohe g’worfn,
sentences.l: Now they set to then and threw him down,
sentences.i: So they set to and threw him down,
sentences.n: “sands hullt her” = sind sie halt her, they came at it, set about it — the phrase says only that they went for him. ohe = herab, g’worfn = geworfen.

sentences.t: und da hot sie san Seel z’thoalt (hat sich seine Seele zertheilt)
sentences.l: and then his soul divided itself (hat sich seine Seele zertheilt)
sentences.i: and then his soul was split into pieces
sentences.n: The Grimms gloss the whole clause this time, not a single word, and their German stands in the brackets as everywhere else: “hat sich seine Seele zertheilt,” his soul divided itself. sie is again the southern reflexive sich, san Seel = seine Seele, z’thoalt = zerteilt (1857 zertheilt).

sentences.t: und is in d’onnen Spiellumpen g’fohrn, döi non (noch) bis date lebnd.
sentences.l: and went into the other gambling-rascals, who still (noch) live to this day.
sentences.i: and passed into the other gambling rogues, who are living yet to this very day.
sentences.n: “is … g’fohrn” = ist gefahren, of a spirit entering someone, as a devil is said to fahren into a man. date = dato, “bis date” = to this day; lebnd = leben. The tale ends by explaining every gambler alive: they have pieces of Spielhansl’s soul in them.

glossary.af: auf — on, onto, up (Bav. af = auf; af d’löst = auf die Letzt)
glossary.d: die — the (Bav. d’ Leut = die Leute, d’ Nacht = die Nacht)
glossary.de: der, die — the (Bav. de Spielhansl = der Spielhansl)
glossary.drin: drinnen — in there, inside (Bav. drin = drinnen)
glossary.en: einen — a, one (Bav. um en Bam = um einen Baum)
glossary.eng: euch — you, to you (Bav. eng = euch)
glossary.fasse: die Fässer — casks, barrels (Bav. d’ Fasse = die Fässer, plural)
glossary.hob: haben — have (Bav., in hob’ns = haben sie)
glossary.holte: behalten — kept (Bav. g’holte; the Grimms gloss it in the text with bei sich behalten)
glossary.holten: behalten — kept (Bav. g’holten; not holen, to fetch)
glossary.hätt: hatte — had (Bav.; here the plain past, not the subjunctive hätte)
glossary.is: ist; es — is; also it (Bav. is does duty for both: Is is = es ist)
glossary.jo: ja — yes; and the particle ja, why, as you see (Bav. jo)
glossary.locken: die Lacke — puddle, pool (Bav. Locken; the Grimms gloss it in the text with Lacken)
glossary.man: mein — my (Bav.; glossed by the Grimms in the text, man (mein) Spielhansl)
glossary.n: ihn; den — him (hobend’n = haben ihn); also the article den (’n Himmel = den Himmel)
glossary.ne: nur — just, only (Bav.; glossed by the Grimms in the text; in “in ne Locken” it is instead the reduced eine)
glossary.ober: aber — but (Bav. ober; also spelt obe)
glossary.of: da, dann — then (Bav.; the same word as Oft with the t dropped in the printing)
glossary.oft: da, dann — then (Bav. oft = da; nothing to do with High German oft, often)
glossary.s: es, das; sie — the clipped enclitic pronoun (hots = hat es, sands = sind sie, s’ Haus = das Haus)
glossary.sann: seinen — his (Bav. dat. pl., mit sann Kortn = mit seinen Karten)
glossary.se: so — so, then (Bav. se, the resuming “then” after a because- or when-clause)
glossary.steigt: steigt — climbs (Bav. affi steigt = hinauf steigt, 3 sg. present of steigen)
glossary.sull: soll — should, is to (Bav. sull = soll)
glossary.un: und — and (Bav. un; also spelt und)
glossary.us: als — than, but, except (Bav. us; ninx us = nichts als; glossed by the Grimms in the text)
glossary.wille: wollen — wanted (Bav., in hot ohi wille = hat hinab wollen)
glossary.willt: wollt — want (Bav. willt’s = wollt ihr, with the pronoun swallowed into the verb)
glossary.wort: warte; das Wort — wait! (imperative, wort nur e Bissl); also Wort, word, and gewartet in g’wort’t
